text.p: Pacific Gas and Electric Co, one of California's largest utilities, said Wednesday it cut its quarterly dividend by $0.19 a share, citing the shift in the electricity industry away from regulated monopolies.
In a statement, the utility said the new dividend of $0.30 a share will be effective with its January 15 payment. The old dividend had been $0.49.
"Over the next five years, a significant portion of our business will be literally transformed from a monopoly to a competitive enterprise," said Stanley Skinner, PG&E's chairman.
He cited California legislation signed in September which clears the way for competition in the industry starting in 1998 as a major milestone in the shift toward competition.
Currently, investor-owned utilities are guaranteed a rate-of-return by regulators based on operating and other costs.

Although California's new law removes many of the uncertainties about the change, it also will mean lower earnings for PG&E than in the past, Skinner noted. In particular, he cited PG&E's need to accelerate depreciation of the Diablo Canyon nuclear power plant as putting pressure on earnings.
"This will mean we will have more expenses to offset revenues and thus less earnings available for the payment of dividends," said Skinner.
Analysts had anticipated a dividend cut since late March when PG&E announced plans to speed the writeoff of Diablo Canyon.
At that time, NatWest Securities Corp. said it expected a dividend cut of at least 50 percent. The actual cut is around 39 percent.
Robin Diedrich, an analyst at Edward Jones, expected a cut of 33 percent, and rated the stock a "hold" at near $20 a share.
PG&E stock was off 1/8 at 23 5/8 late on Wednesday.

Although the California law provides for utilities to recoup investments made prior to deregulation and resolves most of the questions surrounding the process, Diedrich said "around $20 is a more feasible range" for PG&E shares at the new dividend rate.
Industry sources also cited merger rumors regarding PG&E as helping to support its share price.
"There are always merger rumors and PG&E is no exception," said Diedrich. "Now that Enova announced plans to merge with Pacific Enterprises there is even more speculation."

Pacific Enterprises, the parent of Southern California Gas Co., and Enova, the parent of San Diego Gas and Electric Co., said Monday they plan to merge by the end of next year. Combination of the two neighboring utilities is expected to present a competitive threat to PG&E as well as Southern California Edison Co, the state's other major investor-owned utility.
Diedrich said other utilities, especially those with high exposure to nuclear costs, are also likely to cut their dividends.
She cited Centerior Energy Corp., Central Maine Power Co. and Nevada Power Co. as among utilities likely to cut their payouts.

PG&E's Skinner said, "We believe the new dividend level is one that can be sustained and, over time, increased based on the financial performance of our transmission and distribution utility and related energy businesses."
"In addition, it will permit PG&E to generate cash to repurchase our common stock, retire debt, and fully pursue new growth opportunities as competition grows."
--D Beasley, Los Angeles bureau + 1 213 955 6761
